title: Zeta transform (sums over subsets): submask enumeration vs Yates' method
problem_statement: Given a function f from the subsets of an n-element ground set to the integers, as a vector of length N = 2^n indexed by bitmasks, compute its zeta transform (sums over subsets) zeta[S] = sum of f[T] over all T subset of S, for every S. Exact integer arithmetic.

input.parameter: n = size of the ground set; the input vector has N = 2^n entries.
input.size_measure: N = 2^n integers (entries in [-9, 9] in the harness, so all sums have O(n) bits and additions are unit cost). Costs are given in n; in the input size N they read Theta(N^(log2 3)) = Theta(N^1.585) vs Theta(N log N).

algorithms.name: submask enumeration (naive)
algorithms.idea: For every set S, enumerate its 2^|S| submasks with t = (t - 1) & S and add up f[t].
algorithms.pseudocode: for S in 0..N-1: acc = 0; t = S; loop: acc += f[t]; if t == 0: break; t = (t - 1) & S; zeta[S] = acc
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(3^n) = Theta(N^(log2 3)): exactly sum over S of 2^|S| = 3^n additions (counted)
algorithms.correctness: Direct evaluation of the definition. The step t -> (t - 1) & S visits every submask of S exactly once, in decreasing order (from t > 0 it goes to the largest submask of S below t; PROOFS.md sections 1 and 3). The count is sum over k of C(n, k) 2^k = 3^n by the binomial theorem.

algorithms.name: Yates' method (fast zeta transform)
algorithms.idea: Process the n elements one at a time: for element i, add g[S without i] into g[S] for every S that contains i. After all n passes, g = zeta f.
algorithms.pseudocode: g = copy(f); for i in 0..n-1: for S in 0..N-1: if S has bit i: g[S] += g[S xor 2^i]
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(n * 2^n) = Theta(N log N): exactly n * 2^(n-1) additions (counted)
algorithms.correctness: Induction on the passes: after the passes for elements 0..i-1, g[S] is the sum of f[T] over the subsets T of S that agree with S on the elements >= i. The pass for element i adds, for S containing i, the sum over the subsets of S without i that agree with it on elements > i, which is exactly the missing half. Equivalently, the zeta matrix is the n-fold Kronecker power of [[1,0],[1,1]] and the passes apply one factor each.

relationship: Theta(3^n) -> Theta(n 2^n) in the ground-set size n, i.e. Theta(N^1.585) -> Theta(N log N) in the input length N = 2^n. Both are polynomial in the input size, so this is T3, not an exponential pair. Its use in fast subset convolution is background (see background).

background.statement: Bjorklund, Husfeldt, Kaski and Koivisto evaluate the subset convolution of two functions on the subsets of an n-element set in O(n^2 2^n) additions and multiplications, via Moebius transform and inversion, against O(3^n) for the straightforward algorithm.

sources.authors: Björklund, A.; Husfeldt, T.; Kaski, P.; Koivisto, M.
sources.title: Fourier meets Möbius: fast subset convolution
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 39th ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC 2007), 67-74

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree on random set functions with values in [-9, 9] for n = 0..8, 10 and 12, 3 trials each, and pass an independent oracle in harness.check that evaluates the definition by scanning all 2^n masks T with T & ~S == 0 (no submask enumeration, no transform): every S for n <= 8 (complete), 64 seeded random S plus the full set for n = 10, 12 (spot check). V2 (measure 'reported', RESEARCH_LOG RL-047 method): the measured quantity is the exact number of additions performed by the unchanged implementations, counted by an instrumented integer type in the harness. Counts equal the closed forms at every n = 0..12 (experiments/2026-10-07b_zeta_transform_counts.py): naive 3^n, Yates n * 2^(n-1). Fits at tolerance 0.02 (the counts are exact and have no lower-order terms, so alpha = 1.000 for both): naive rivals n*2^n 1.315, n*3^n 0.886, 4^n 0.792, all rejected; Yates rivals 2^n 1.161, n^2*2^n 0.877, 3^n 0.733, all rejected. The log-factor diagnostic is resolved for Yates (0.936 against n log n 2^n). Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of this entry from the code (the correctness of both algorithms, the time and space bounds, the exact counts for all sizes of their domains, the value sizes) and names the scripts and tests that check each one, among them tests/test_proofs_zeta.py.

caveats: Costs count additions on integers with O(n) bits (bounded entries); index arithmetic and loop control are not counted. Counts measure arithmetic, not wall-clock time; timing would not resolve the log factor (RESEARCH_LOG RL-048). The name 'Yates' method' refers to Yates (1937), a book on factorial experiments that was not checked here; the algorithm's correctness is proved in this entry, not taken from that source.
notes: Same Kronecker-power structure as the fast Walsh-Hadamard transform (xor-convolution-naive-vs-walsh-hadamard), with the 2x2 matrix [[1,0],[1,1]] in place of [[1,1],[1,-1]]. Its inverse, the Moebius transform, uses [[1,0],[-1,1]] and also costs n 2^(n-1) operations. Subset convolution (straightforward 3^n vs n^2 2^n) is not part of this entry; research/2026-10-07_patterns.md records that the V2 slope test could not separate those two cost claims at n <= 13 (rho = 1.205, analytic; alpha = 0.836 measured against 3^n).
